title: VPNs and Tunnels
oneLiner: What a VPN actually does to your packets, what someone on café Wi-Fi can still see, full versus split tunnel, and site-to-site versus remote access.
keyTakeaway: A VPN wraps your packets inside encrypted packets addressed to a VPN server, which unwraps them and sends them on. The local network sees only the tunnel. It joins you to a private network and protects data in transit, but it doesn't make an infected device safe.
explanation:
A VPN (virtual private network) builds a tunnel: each packet you send is encrypted and wrapped inside a new outer packet addressed to a VPN server. Anyone on the network in between, such as café Wi-Fi or a hotel, sees only encrypted packets going to that one server. The server decrypts them and forwards the original packets as if your device were plugged in on its side. That's how a laptop at home reaches private addresses like 10.10.5.20 that aren't routed on the internet at all.

A remote-access VPN connects one device (with a client such as WireGuard, an IPsec client built into the operating system, or a vendor's SSL VPN client) to a company network. A site-to-site VPN permanently joins two networks through their firewalls, for example two plants, so devices on either side need no VPN software. With a full tunnel all of the laptop's traffic goes through the company; with split tunnel only company addresses do and everything else goes straight out, which saves bandwidth but skips the company's web filtering.

Two common misunderstandings. Without a VPN, HTTPS already protects the content of web traffic, but the destination address and usually the hostname are still visible to the local network. And a VPN protects the path, not the endpoint: an infected laptop on a VPN carries the malware straight into the network. That's why VPNs are paired with multi-factor authentication (MFA), device checks and rules limiting what VPN users can reach, and why zero trust network access (ZTNA), which grants access per application rather than per network, is replacing them in many companies.
